title: Symmetric matrices, perpendicular eigenvectors
objectives: Use the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices.
Write a symmetric matrix as $\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$ and as a sum of rank-one pieces.

screens.title: A direction that only stretches
screens.prose: The matrix $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ sends $\mathbf{v}$ to $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$. Drag the head of $\mathbf{v}$ and watch $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$ follow. The shaded line runs through $\mathbf{v}$.
screens.question: Which $\mathbf{v}$ has its image $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$ on the shaded line?

options.why: You read the 2 on the diagonal as a stretch of $(1, 0)$. But $\mathbf{A}(1, 0) = (2, 1)$, which leaves the line.
You picked an image that is longer, but it has also turned. $(4, 5)$ is not a multiple of $(1, 2)$.
You stopped too soon. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ onto the diagonal and look again.

hints.text: Try arrows whose two entries are equal.
Drag $\mathbf{v}$ onto the diagonal $y = x$.
At $\mathbf{v} = (1, 1)$: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = (2 + 1, 1 + 2) = (3, 3) = 3\mathbf{v}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ until $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$ lies on the shaded line.

explain.text: You found $\mathbf{v} = (1, 1)$, where $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = 3\mathbf{v}$. So $(1, 1)$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3. Every multiple of it works too.

screens.title: The second direction
screens.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ only stretches one more direction. The green arrow marks the first one, $(1, 1)$. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ round until $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$ again lands on the shaded line.
screens.question: What angle does the second direction make with $(1, 1)$?

options.why: You stopped at $(1, 0)$ or $(0, 1)$, 45° from $(1, 1)$. Their images leave the shaded line.
You found $(-1, -1)$. That is the same line as $(1, 1)$, just reversed. Look for a new line.
You did not try the other diagonal. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ to $(1, -1)$.

hints.text: Try the other diagonal, through $(1, -1)$.
At $\mathbf{v} = (1, -1)$, compute $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$.

feedback.correct: $(1, -1)$ is the second direction, at a right angle to $(1, 1)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ to $(1, -1)$ and read the caption.

explain.text: At $(1, -1)$ you saw $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = (1, -1) = \mathbf{v}$: eigenvalue 1. The dot product $(1, 1) \cdot (1, -1) = 1 - 1 = 0$. The two eigenvectors are perpendicular.

screens.title: Eigenvectors as a basis
screens.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ equals its own transpose: it is **symmetric**. Scale its eigenvectors to length 1: $\mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)$ and $\mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-1, 1)$. As the columns of $\mathbf{Q}$ they form an orthonormal basis.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}$.

hints.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}$ has columns $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_1 = 3\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_2 = \mathbf{q}_2$.
Entry $(i, j)$ of $\mathbf{Q}^T(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q})$ is $\mathbf{q}_i$ dotted with column $j$ of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}$.
$\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot 3\mathbf{q}_1 = 3$, $\mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{q}_2 = 1$, and every $\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{q}_2$ is 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_1 = 3\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_2 = \mathbf{q}_2$, then take dot products.

byKey.r0c1: Your top-left entry is off. It is $\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_1 = 3\,\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{q}_1 = 3$.
byKey.r0c2: Your off-diagonal entry is not 0. It is $\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{q}_2$ times an eigenvalue, and $\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{q}_2 = 0$.
byKey.r1c1: Your off-diagonal entry is not 0. It is $\mathbf{q}_2 \cdot 3\mathbf{q}_1$, and $\mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{q}_1 = 0$.
byKey.r1c2: Your bottom-right entry is off. It is $\mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_2 = \mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{q}_2 = 1$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}$ has columns $3\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$. Multiplying by $\mathbf{Q}^T$ takes dot products with $\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$: 1 on the diagonal, 0 off it. So $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}$, the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues.

screens.title: An inverse for free
screens.prose: To get $\mathbf{A}$ back from $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}$, we must undo $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{Q}^T$. So we need $\mathbf{Q}^{-1}$. Its columns are orthonormal, so look before you start eliminating.
screens.question: Which matrix is $\mathbf{Q}^{-1}$?

options.why: You inverted each entry. An inverse undoes the whole map, not each number: this times $\mathbf{Q}$ has a 4 in the corner.
You used $\mathbf{Q}$ itself. $\mathbf{Q}$ turns the plane by 45°, and turning twice gives 90°, not $\mathbf{I}$.
You flipped every sign. That turns by 225°, and $-\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q} = -\mathbf{Q}^2$ is not $\mathbf{I}$.

hints.text: What is $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ when the columns of $\mathbf{Q}$ are orthonormal?
Entry $(i, j)$ of $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ is $\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{q}_j$.
$\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{q}_j$ is 1 when $i = j$ and 0 otherwise, so $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the matrix whose rows dot with the columns of $\mathbf{Q}$ to give $\mathbf{I}$.

explain.text: The rows of $\mathbf{Q}^T$ are $\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$, so $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ holds their dot products: $\mathbf{I}$. No elimination needed. Undoing both sides gives $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$.

screens.title: One piece per direction
screens.prose: Multiply out $\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$ column by row: $$\mathbf{A} = \lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T + \lambda_2\mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^T$$ Each $\mathbf{q}\mathbf{q}^T$ is a rank-one matrix. Now build a new matrix $\mathbf{C}$ with eigenvalue 5 along $\mathbf{q}_1$ and 1 along $\mathbf{q}_2$.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{C} = 5\,\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T + 1\,\mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^T$.

hints.text: Scale the first piece by 5 and the second by 1, then add.
Every entry of $\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}$. The second piece has $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ off the diagonal.
Diagonal: $5 \times \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 3$. Off the diagonal: $5 \times \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2} = 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $5 \times$ the first piece to $1 \times$ the second, entry by entry.

byKey.r0c1: Your diagonal entry is off: $5 \times \tfrac{1}{2} + 1 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 3$. Each piece carries a $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
byKey.r1c2: Your diagonal entry is off: $5 \times \tfrac{1}{2} + 1 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 3$. Each piece carries a $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
byKey.r0c2: Your off-diagonal entry is off. The second piece subtracts there: $5 \times \tfrac{1}{2} - 1 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 2$.
byKey.r1c1: Your off-diagonal entry is off. The second piece subtracts there: $5 \times \tfrac{1}{2} - 1 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 2$.

explain.text: You scaled each rank-one piece by its eigenvalue and added. Check: $\mathbf{C}(1, 1) = (5, 5)$ and $\mathbf{C}(-1, 1) = (-1, 1)$. Choosing perpendicular directions and two numbers fixed a symmetric matrix.

screens.title: Two equal eigenvalues
screens.prose: Same pieces, but give both directions the eigenvalue 4. Then $\mathbf{D} = 4\,\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T + 4\,\mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^T = 4(\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T + \mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^T)$. Add the two pieces first.
screens.question: Which vectors are eigenvectors of $\mathbf{D}$?

options.why: You kept the directions you built with. But the pieces add to $\mathbf{I}$, so $\mathbf{D} = 4\mathbf{I}$ stretches everything by 4.
You read $\mathbf{D}$ as diagonal and stopped at the axes. $4\mathbf{I}$ stretches every arrow, not only those.

options.text: None: the theorem needs distinct eigenvalues
options.why: You expected a repeated eigenvalue to break things. $4\mathbf{I}$ still has perpendicular eigenvectors: any pair will do.

hints.text: Add $\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T$ and $\mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^T$ entry by entry.
The $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ off the diagonal cancel.
The pieces add to $\mathbf{I}$, so $\mathbf{D} = 4\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{D}\mathbf{v} = 4\mathbf{v}$ for every $\mathbf{v}$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{D} = 4\mathbf{I}$, so every non-zero vector is an eigenvector.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two pieces and see what $\mathbf{D}$ is.

explain.text: The pieces sum to $\mathbf{I}$, so $\mathbf{D} = 4\mathbf{I}$. With a repeated eigenvalue the eigen-directions fill a whole plane. Any orthonormal pair in it can serve as $\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$.

screens.title: A matrix that is not symmetric
screens.prose: Now take $\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, which is not symmetric. Its eigenvalues are 2 and 3, distinct and real. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ to find both directions that $\mathbf{B}$ only stretches.
screens.question: What angle do the two eigen-directions of $\mathbf{B}$ make?

options.why: You assumed two distinct eigenvalues force a right angle. That needs symmetry. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ to $(1, 0)$, then to $(1, 1)$.
You found $(1, 0)$ and stopped. Two distinct eigenvalues give two directions: try $(1, 1)$.

hints.text: Start with $\mathbf{v} = (1, 0)$. Then try the diagonal.
$\mathbf{B}(1, 0) = (2, 0)$. Where does $(1, 1)$ go?
$\mathbf{B}(1, 1) = (3, 3)$. The directions $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$ meet at 45°.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ to $(1, 0)$ and to $(1, 1)$ and compare.

byKey.perp: You assumed two distinct eigenvalues force a right angle. Only a symmetric matrix promises that. $\mathbf{B}$'s eigenvectors $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$ are 45° apart.

explain.text: $\mathbf{B}(1, 0) = (2, 0)$ and $\mathbf{B}(1, 1) = (3, 3)$. The dot product $(1, 0) \cdot (1, 1) = 1$ is not 0, so the angle is 45°. Real, distinct eigenvalues are not enough: perpendicular needs $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{B}^T$.

screens.title: The spectral theorem
screens.prose: Both symmetric matrices had perpendicular eigenvectors, and $\mathbf{B}$ did not. The **spectral theorem**: a real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors, so $$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T = \lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T + \lambda_2\mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^T$$ with $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$.
screens.question: Which matrix is sure to have orthonormal eigenvectors?

options.why: You saw distinct real eigenvalues, 2 and $-1$, and stopped. Without symmetry the eigenvectors $(1, 0)$ and $(2, -3)$ are not perpendicular.
You may have taken the zeros on the diagonal as a good sign. This is a quarter turn: no real direction is only stretched.
You matched the diagonal and ignored the corners. 1 and 2 differ, so this is not symmetric.

hints.text: Compare each matrix with its transpose.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The theorem needs $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}^T$: the two off-diagonal entries must match.

explain.text: Its eigenvalues are 3 and $-2$, with eigenvectors $(2, 1)$ and $(1, -2)$: perpendicular, as promised. The triangular matrix has real eigenvalues but slanted eigenvectors. The quarter turn has no real eigenvalues at all.

screens.title: Why perpendicular
screens.prose: Take $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}^T$ with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1$, $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2$ and $\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2$. We slide $\mathbf{A}$ from one side of the dot product to the other.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

hints.text: Start from $\lambda_1$ and finish with $\lambda_2$.
Symmetry is used once, after the transpose appears.
Eigenvector, transpose, symmetry, eigenvector, then subtract the two ends.

feedback.correct: Symmetry carried $\mathbf{A}$ across the dot product.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with $\lambda_1$, write the dot product as a transpose, use symmetry, then reach $\lambda_2$.

byKey.symmetric: You used symmetry before there was an $\mathbf{A}^T$ to replace. Write $(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1)^T$ as $\mathbf{v}_1^T\mathbf{A}^T$ first.
byKey.conclude: The conclusion needs both ends: $\lambda_1(\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2)$ and $\lambda_2(\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2)$. Put it last.

explain.text: Only one line used symmetry: replacing $\mathbf{A}^T$ by $\mathbf{A}$. For $\mathbf{B}$ in the trap that line fails, and so does the conclusion. With equal eigenvalues the last line says nothing, and we choose perpendicular eigenvectors ourselves.

screens.title: Perpendicular portfolios
screens.prose: A risk model gives two stocks' daily covariance matrix, in $\%^2$: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}1.1&0.3\\0.3&1.9\end{pmatrix}$. A covariance matrix is always symmetric. One eigenvector is the portfolio with weights $(1, 3)$.
screens.question: Without solving anything, which is the other eigen-direction?

options.why: You flipped one sign. $(1, 3) \cdot (1, -3) = 1 - 9 = -8$, not 0.
You swapped the entries without a sign change. $(1, 3) \cdot (3, 1) = 6$, not 0.
That is $(1, 3)$ reversed: the same line, not a new direction.

hints.text: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is symmetric. What does the spectral theorem say about its eigenvectors?
You need a direction with zero dot product with $(1, 3)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the direction whose dot product with $(1, 3)$ is 0.

explain.text: Symmetry made the second eigenvector perpendicular, with no algebra. Check: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(1, 3) = (2.0, 6.0)$, eigenvalue 2.0, and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(3, -1) = (3.0, -1.0)$, eigenvalue 1.0. Splitting risk into perpendicular portfolios like these is where PCA starts.

ideas: A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors. Without symmetry, eigenvectors can slant.
Unit eigenvectors as the columns of $\mathbf{Q}$ give $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$, and $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T$ costs nothing.
Column by row, $\mathbf{A} = \sum_i \lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T$: one rank-one piece per eigen-direction.

formula.name: Spectral theorem
formula.note: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$: the columns of $\mathbf{Q}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors.

summary.trap: Distinct real eigenvalues do not make eigenvectors perpendicular: $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvectors 45° apart. Symmetry does.

quiz.question: What is the top-right entry of $\mathbf{Q}^{-1}$?

widget.label: Top-right entry of the inverse
widget.accept: 0.8: $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T$, whose top-right entry is the bottom-left of $\mathbf{Q}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Orthonormal columns give $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T$.

byKey.copied: You copied the entry of $\mathbf{Q}$. The inverse is the transpose: its top-right is $\mathbf{Q}$'s bottom-left.
byKey.recip: You took $1/(-0.8)$. An inverse matrix is not the reciprocal of each entry.

explain.text: The columns are orthonormal: $0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 1$ and $(0.6)(-0.8) + (0.8)(0.6) = 0$. So $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T = \begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.8\\-0.8&0.6\end{pmatrix}$.

quiz.prose: A symmetric $\mathbf{A}$ has eigenvalue 4 along $\mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)$ and eigenvalue 2 along $\mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, -1)$.
quiz.question: What is the off-diagonal entry of $\mathbf{A}$?

byKey.diag: That is the diagonal entry, $4 \times \tfrac{1}{2} + 2 \times \tfrac{1}{2}$. Off the diagonal the second piece subtracts.
byKey.no-half: You left out the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in each $\mathbf{q}\mathbf{q}^T$: $4 - 2 = 2$. Each unit vector carries $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
byKey.sum: You added the eigenvalues. Their sum, 6, is the sum of the diagonal entries.

explain.text: $\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T$ has every entry $\tfrac{1}{2}$, and $\mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^T$ has $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ off the diagonal. So $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$. Check: $\mathbf{A}(1, 1) = (4, 4)$ and $\mathbf{A}(1, -1) = (2, -2)$.

options.text: Every non-zero vector is an eigenvector, and any orthonormal pair can be $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2$

options.why: You read the eigenvectors off the diagonal shape. $7\mathbf{I}$ stretches every vector by 7.

options.text: The spectral theorem fails: the eigenvalues repeat
options.why: You took distinct eigenvalues as a condition of the theorem. It is only a condition of the perpendicularity proof.
You may have looked for a single special direction. Every direction is special here.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}$ for any $\mathbf{v}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = 7\mathbf{v}$ for every $\mathbf{v}$, so every non-zero vector is an eigenvector. Any rotation $\mathbf{Q}$ gives $\mathbf{Q}(7\mathbf{I})\mathbf{Q}^T = 7\mathbf{I}$. A repeated eigenvalue leaves us free to choose the orthonormal pair.

quiz.prose: Each matrix has two distinct real eigenvalues.
quiz.question: Which one has eigenvectors that are not perpendicular?

options.why: You may have been put off by the uneven diagonal. This one is symmetric, so its eigenvectors are perpendicular.
A diagonal matrix is symmetric. Its eigenvectors are the axes, at 90°.
You may have read the negative entries as a problem. They match, so this is symmetric: eigenvectors $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the matrix that is not equal to its transpose.

explain.text: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ sends $(1, 0)$ to itself and $(1, 1)$ to $(2, 2)$. Those eigenvectors have dot product 1, so they are not perpendicular. The other three are symmetric.
